questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere much different to where I had been before

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked Korea, but going on exchange is a lengthy, and sometimes stressful, process, especially when it comes to certain required documents, and this process isn't done just because you've arrived in the country.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. I had researched general stuff like transport beforehand, and I learned most of the school related stuff quickly

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an orientation for foreign students, detailing everything about campus life, rules, clubs, and such. here we also received a guide book and a map of campus, which was very useful for getting around at first.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They went over most things at the orientation, and the rest could be found in the extra guide.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I stayed at SK Global House, which is a mixed dorm on campus offering both double- and single-rooms. I stayed in a single room, where there was a bed, a desk, some closet space, and a bathroom. It also had large windows for fresh air, which is more than you can say about most goshiwons. The monthly rent was the same as my dormitory in Denmark, however, it's a lot smaller.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There is a common area on each floor with a microwave oven. There is also a larger kitchen on one of the basement floors, but I never used it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is by far the most convenient option, both because it's close to the school, but also because the application is pretty simple compared to other options. A drawback is the many rules. Global House is apparantly the dorm with least rules on campus, but it's still more stringent than what many are used to if you've lived in Danish dormitories. just read the rules and try not to break them. It gets noisy, which can be pretty annoying, especially if your neighbour happens to have coughing fits every night for 4 months straight. one negative about the location is, that it's pretty far from everything else, since it's in the top right corner of the campus. there are of course a few restaurants and cafes nearby, but it takes 20 minutes to walk to Shinchon, the main area close by, maybe a bit less if you're lucky with catching a bus at the right time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall it had what it needed. one thing to note is that it was pretty dirty when I took over the room. keep this in mind and maybe buy some cleaning stuff at Daiso when moving in. There are a lot of mosquitoes in the summer and they are vicious

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: super complicated process, added to this, were a bunch of technical difficulties on the university's side, making for an overall stressful experience.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: there are like three stages. in the first you bid some points on the courses you want, and after not getting them you move on the the next stage. stage two is first come first serve on the remaining courses, but actually you don't really know if the courses will be cancelled until the registration process is over. sometimes they also increase the number of seats, if classes have many applicants. you just don't know which is the case until the registration process is over. I think there's a third stage, but I got the courses I wanted after the first two. as a last resort, you can write specific teachers for courses you didn't get, and maybe you can still get in.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: you get an email with information about the process. read it carefully, because it's hard to understand. you can of course write the university for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: By some crazy stroke of luck I managed to get all of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you're on exchange for the experience rather than the academics, you may consider tailoring your schedule to that. I took four courses, and they were all on Mondays and Wednesdays, meaning I had more time to travel or look around seoul. Exams are usually held instead of classes, so doing this means, you'll probably have to take several exams in one day.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not a lot of courses for my major. some courses were taught in English, but didn't allow foreign students for some reason. meanwhile many courses that did allow foreign students were only taught in Korean. This locked a student like me out of many courses, and I had to be more creative with the courses I chose.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think the level was okay. each course is smaller than the ones in Denmark, so expect them to have a slightly smaller syllabus as well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: some courses were just listening-lectures, while others had more class participation. at UCPH we have smaller classes to supplement lectures, but that doesn't exist here. this gives you more free time, but it also means you'll have to study a bit more yourself if you want to do well. I found that the subjects in the international student category were a bit easier than the regular courses, use that information how you will. like at UCPH, buying books is optional, it really depends on the subject and exam structure, which vary widely.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Real Estate Finance and Economics
Principles of Marketing
Money, Banking and Finance
Cosmopolitanism and Critics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend Priciples of marketing for anyone even slightly interested in the topic. it's an introductory course, so it should be easy to follow for most people, and I personally found it pretty interesting.
Also, only take Real Estate Finance and Economics if you are really interested in the topic. I thought it sounded kind of interesting. I was Wrong.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: ARC-fee, I didn't know you had to pay for that

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: restaurants are very cheap and the food is very good

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of the club activities involved drinking, so if you're not into that options are more limited. They do exist, there just isn't as many of them.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Mentors Club: Korean students arrange meetups with bigger groups of foreign students. all foreigners join this club. these groups will go eating, clubbing, or whatever activities they may decide on. in my experience it dies out after the first couple of months, but it's a good way to meet other foreign students.
International Club: host a few group activities. I think you can participate in up to two. Each activity usually happens three times in a semester, they include: movie night, game night, seoul exploration, dance class, and a couple others.
Buddy Programme: A foreigner is assigned a Korean "Buddy", they can do activities and exchange languages with. this is poorly advertised, and apparently it starts pretty late on in the semester.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Any of the above mentioned. Just building some relationships from the get-go is really helpful. if you get a Korean friend or too that is also extremely helpful to experience the culture from the Korean perspective, whic is very interesting.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit Busan or Jeju. the east coast is nice if you like the ocean. Suwon is pretty close to Seoul. Gapyeong is a bit further away, but is close to Nami Island, which is a tourist hotspot, and the area also has some great dakgalbi. Of course there are plenty of things to see in Seoul as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, being nice and respectful until you understand the gist of the culture is helpful

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: join clubs, that's usually where Korean students wanting foreign friends go. there are also apps, which can get you in contact with locals, but you probably know those already. many Koreans are interested in talking to foreigners because they want to improve their english.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The drivers can be pretty crazy. I don't usually get car sick, but riding Korean busses and Taxis have made me reevaluate that part of my identity. bicycles don't always have their designated lanes and will use the walkway instead, and being aware of this was something I had to get used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: It's very clean. people don't just throw their trash in the street, and will instead carry it around until they find a trash can, which are very rare in Korea.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Prepare beforehand when it comes to transport, courses, and things you want to see.
Try new things. there are plenty of entertainment options which you may see as niche and weird, but which turn out to be really fun when you actually try it. clubs and such can help introduce you to that. also, there is so much good food, and going out eating with a Korean will show so many more options. 
At some point you have to apply for the ARC. this can be done through the school, which should be simpler, but I'm not sure it is. Reading up on that before going would be a good idea, to make sure you have, or can get, all the required documents easily.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get apps like Naver/Kakao maps, Kakao T(for Taxi service), Kakao Talk (messaging app, used by all Koreans, register account as soon as possible, you'll need it right at the beginning), Papago (translating text and images), Y-attend (used at Yonsei to check attendance status.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being on my own in an unknown culture helped me grow a lot, and it gave me many experiences I wouldn't want to be without. Going on exchange has been one of the best decisions of my life, so I do recommend it to anyone interested.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I got lonely from time to time, since I didn't have my family or friends with me, but getting out and exploring the country really helped me get through that and made the experience much better.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Korea is a great destination for exchange. It's clean, safe, and has plenty to offer.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
